summary: Nearly every nationality must obtain a visa from a Central African embassy before travel — only citizens of fellow CEMAC states (Cameroon, Chad, Congo, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea) enter visa-free — and most governments currently advise against all travel to the country because of armed conflict.

notes: Export of rough diamonds, gold and other minerals without a license is strictly prohibited.
Photography of government buildings, airports and anything military is forbidden without a permit.

payments.text: This is a cash-only economy for visitors. Cards are accepted almost nowhere and ATMs in Bangui are few and unreliable. Bring enough CFA francs (or euros to exchange) for your whole stay.

safety.text: Most governments advise against all travel to the Central African Republic. Armed groups control parts of the country, and violent crime, kidnapping and sudden outbreaks of fighting are real risks even in Bangui. Any travel should be organized with professional security support.

bestTimeToVisit.text: December to February, the heart of the dry season, offers the most passable roads and access to Dzanga-Sangha in the far southwest; the rains from May to October make much of the country unreachable.

tips.text: Check your government's travel advice before even planning a trip — most currently advise against all travel to the Central African Republic, and insurance policies are often void in do-not-travel zones.

There is no eVisa and no visa on arrival. The visa must be obtained in advance from a Central African embassy (Paris, Brussels, Washington and several African capitals). Diplomatic representation is thin, so plan weeks ahead.

The one destination that draws travelers — Dzanga-Sangha's lowland gorillas and forest elephants — is only realistically visited on a fully organized trip via the park's official operators, usually entering through Bangui.
Bring all the money you will need in cash (CFA francs or euros to exchange). Cards and ATMs cannot be relied on anywhere in the country.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for the Central African Republic?
faq.answer: Yes, unless you hold a passport from a CEMAC state (Cameroon, Chad, Congo, Gabon or Equatorial Guinea). Everyone else must obtain a visa in advance from a Central African embassy. There is no eVisa and no visa on arrival.

faq.question: How do I get a Central African Republic visa?
faq.answer: Apply in person or by mail at a Central African embassy — Paris, Brussels and Washington handle most Western applicants, and there are missions in several African capitals. Expect to provide a letter of invitation or hotel booking, a yellow fever certificate and a return ticket; allow several weeks.

faq.question: Is the Central African Republic safe to visit?
faq.answer: No — most governments advise against all travel. Armed groups remain active across much of the country and the security situation can deteriorate quickly, including in Bangui. The few travelers who visit Dzanga-Sangha do so on fully organized trips with security arrangements.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever vaccination for the Central African Republic?
faq.answer: Yes. A yellow fever certificate is required for all travelers aged 9 months and over and is checked on arrival in Bangui.

faq.question: Which nationalities can enter the Central African Republic without a visa?
faq.answer: Citizens of the CEMAC bloc — Cameroon, Chad, the Republic of the Congo, Gabon and Equatorial Guinea — enter visa-free under the Community's free-movement arrangements. All other nationalities need an embassy visa.
